newsitem.title: UK: Job figures, new plant, boost N.Ireland economy.
newsitem.headline: Job figures, new plant, boost N.Ireland economy.

text.p: Northern Ireland announced another fall in unemployment and a 78 million pound ($123 million) job creating expansion on Wednesday as the province adjusted to a rare patch of peace.
The government said that seasonally adjusted unemployment fell by 2,100 to 60,500 in July, or 7.9 percent of the workforce, from 11.3 percent in July 1996.
Unadjusted unemployment rose in real terms by 4,336 to 65,135 but fell proportionally to 8.5 percent of the labour force from 11.8 a year ago, the department of economic development said.

The figures, which confirmed a downward trend stretching back for more than a year, were released on the day that a U.S. multinational announced a major expansion in the province's second city, Londonderry.
Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam said Dupont was setting up a new state of the art automated plant to meet European demand for the fabric lycra.
The 78 million pound expansion will also secure 450 jobs at Dupont's Maydown site, the largest Lycra fibre production operation in Europe.
Mowlam said in a statement that the expansion showed Northern Ireland was "a good place to do business".

"It is particularly important because it is one of the strongest signals ever by a leader of corporate America to the international business community, especially in the United States, of the strength of Northern Ireland's business case."
DuPont (UK) managing director Bill Walker said: "This expansion represents our continued confidence in both the European market and our operations in Northern Ireland."
DuPont employs almost 1,000 people in Londonderry since it chose Northern Ireland in 1960 and is one of the biggest exporters in the province.

The scheme was announced weeks after the Irish Republican Army (IRA) announced a new truce in its 28-year war against British rule in an attempt to get its political wing, Sinn Fein, to peace talks in September.
Britain says Northern Ireland's economy has proved robust and has in many sectors shrugged off the effects of three decades of political and sectarian conflict that killed 3,200 people.
It says that the Northern Ireland economy, once a regional black spot, is now performing as well as many other British regions and better than most.
But business leaders say it could attract further foreign investment if pro-British and pro-Irish political groups join the September peace talks.

Sinn Fein says it will be there when the talks open on September 15 but the province's key Protestant group, the Ulster Unionist Party, has not made clear whether it will negotiate with Sinn Fein or not.
It says the July 20 truce is a ruse and that the IRA will go back to war if it does not get the kind of settlement it seeks. ($ = 0.633 British Pounds)
